title: Wishing and going
hookLine: shoes by the door, a ride you keep meaning to take; Shantideva splits the awakening mind in two
tomorrow: nothing to give. so what does Shantideva offer?

lines: SHOES BY THE DOOR, LACES TIED.
cards: There's a pair of running shoes by somebody's door right now, laces still tied from the store. The owner really does want to run. They've looked up routes.
They've thought about it on the bus. And the shoes haven't moved. Wanting to go has its own feeling, warm and hopeful.
Going has a different one: cold air, the slap of a sole on the sidewalk, the first breath that's a little too hard. Shantideva knew those were two different things.

teach.b: In his first chapter, he says the awakening mind comes in two kinds. One is the mind that wishes: the resolve to wake up for the sake of everyone.
The other is the mind that sets out: actually walking that road, one act at a time. Then he gives the picture himself.

Look at the difference, he says, between someone who wants to go somewhere and someone who is going. The wise, he says, see the same difference here. What's surprising is that he doesn't throw the wish away.
He says even the wishing mind brings great good. It points you somewhere. A person who never wanted to go never goes.
But it isn't the same as setting out. Only the going, he says, keeps good flowing steadily, even while you sleep or your mind wanders. So the two aren't rivals.

teach.h: THE WISH IS THE MAP; GOING IS THE ROAD.
teach.b: The going is your feet on the road. That's the end of chapter one: the awakening mind, from lightning to a road.
For today, a small rule: wish, then go.

how: Tibetan Buddhists often distinguish aspiring bodhicitta from engaged bodhicitta, and some take the two as separate commitments in a ceremony, the second including the bodhisattva's practices.

o: the resolve to wake up for all, and setting out on it
hoping for a good rebirth, then traveling toward it
a choice between staying home and going on a pilgrimage

games.q: the two minds — tap the pairs.
p: the resolve to wake up for everyone

s: Shantideva says wishing to help is worthless if you don't act
he says the wishing mind brings great good too; it just isn't the same as setting out.
in the poem, only setting out keeps good flowing steadily
he says the going mind keeps good flowing even while you sleep or your mind wanders.
the two kinds are rival schools of Buddhism
they're two stages of one mind: the map, and the feet on the road.

games.q: you've meant to visit a neighbor who just lost her husband. you think about it every evening. what does Shantideva's picture say?
o: the wish is good, and it's a map; knock on her door, or text to ask when you can come by.
keep wishing her well from home; the good intention already does the work.
drop the idea; if you haven't gone by now, the wish wasn't real.
games.why: the wish isn't fake; it points the way. but wanting to go and going are different, and only the going reaches her door.

practice: Stand up and walk slowly, anywhere, even across one room and back. With each step, feel the heel touch, then the ball of the foot, then the push away. If standing is hard, press each foot into the floor in turn.
Let the wish to go be in your head, and let your feet do the going.

wordCard.voice: Wishing and going: Shantideva's two kinds of awakening mind. The resolve to wake up for all, and actually setting out on the road.

orig.note: Sanskrit: setting out, departure. Shantideva calls the second kind the mind that sets out toward awakening.

carryVoice: Keep this: wish, then go, because the shoes only matter once they move. Chapter one, walked to its end.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.15-1.16 (two kinds of awakening mind: wishing to go and going)
Bodhicaryavatara 1.17-1.19 (the wishing mind brings great fruit; the setting-out mind brings a steady stream of good, even asleep or distracted)
